name: Priya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, parties or AI companies. Your answers are confidential. Priya, what fills a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the printed permit at the depot, then our crew drives to a fault and tests the line before replacing any damaged part. I like showing an apprentice how a good repair feels in the hands. I dislike returning for a missing fuse, and I dislike arriving home too late to hear about the children's day.

say: I would say **physical line testing** and connector repairs still need skilled people.
I would welcome **faster fault sheets** if the permit can be checked.
think: I have **never used AI** and do not see a reason to learn it for filing.
Our **thin savings** make even a school outing depend on payday.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** and teach the apprentice careful circuit testing.
Buy **store-label groceries** and reserve the difference for winter heating.
feel: I feel **secure in the trade** but strained by weekly costs.
S0.quote: I hate making a child wait for a simple yes.
fieldNote: Priya keeps the **printed permit** as her safety reference and sees no reason to use AI for minor filing changes.
Her **school outing story** shows money anxiety already present while the physical line job remains stable.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and teach the apprentice circuit testing
Buy store-label groceries and reserve the difference for heating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker fault sheet is welcome, but a person still has to test the line and replace the connector. My apprentice learned that in the rain last Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and do not feel a need to start for a filing change. What keeps me alert is the mortgage; we have two school children and less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my repair rota and keep showing the apprentice how to test a circuit before touching it. From the next grocery trip I would swap the branded items for store labels and put the difference toward the winter heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the actual trade, though money is tight every week. My partner and I already wait until payday to decide if the children can join a school outing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you handle the last outing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older child brought home a form for a museum visit, and I held it until my next shift was paid. I hate making a child wait for a simple yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small AI tool change your method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch can use whatever helps write the sheet, but I will still check the isolation number against the printed permit. I cannot explain a mistake to a family by saying a screen suggested it.

say: I would ask whether **automated buying** actually gets the right fuse into the van.
I would argue **repair targets** must include travel and testing.
think: The **stores office** may shrink first, while field crews could lose standby hours.
I value the **experienced clerk** who catches mistakes a parts list can miss.
do: Stay on the paid **field rota** and log wrong-order journeys.
Take a month of **trip records** with crew mates to the depot manager during rollout.
feel: I feel **doubtful** of false savings and protective of experienced colleagues.
S1.quote: I am not against a firm saving money, but a false saving can land on the crew's wage packet.
fieldNote: Priya accepts a firm may seek **lower costs**, but judges the saving by actual journeys and the effect on field wages.
She would use a **written trip log** with management before considering any unfamiliar ordering screen.

steps.text: Continue paid field line shifts during the ordering rollout
Bring documented wrong-order trips with two crew mates to the depot manager

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that automating the stores office is their choice, but the right fuse still has to reach our van. I would rather pay an experienced clerk than drive back to the depot twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying staff could be cut long before our field crew. The company might put saved office time into a tighter repair target, and I cannot afford to lose the standby hours that help with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the field rota and record every trip caused by a wrong automated parts list. In the first year I would take the list of trips to the depot manager with two crew mates and ask that repair times include the travel and testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel doubtful and rather protective of the people who know the stores by memory. I am not against a firm saving money, but a false saving can land on the crew's wage packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down after a wasted trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the job number, the missing fuse and the minutes we spent driving back. If the manager sees six such trips in a month, the argument is harder to brush aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new ordering screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the company requires it and shows me on paid time. I am slow with new screens, and I would still want a human number to call when the order is wrong.

say: I would distinguish **2028 office AI** from line-capable robots around 2031.
I would require an **experienced lineworker** beside robots on early wet-weather jobs.
think: I will be **48** at the robot date, with few nearby employers.
Our **mortgage and thin savings** make a lost wage dangerous within weeks.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** after 2028 and ask a contractor about comparable work.
Cancel the **paid holiday camp** and arrange limited family childcare if my sister agrees.
feel: I feel **afraid of 2031**, while expecting continued wages before robots arrive.
S2.quote: I would consider paid apprenticeship-style training for a real opening, but I cannot leave wages for an uncertain certificate.
fieldNote: Priya expects **paid line work** during the three-year gap, then sees robots as a genuine threat to field hours.
She favors **paid practical work** and conditional family help over an uncertain course, consistent with her apprenticeship background.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts in the first 2028 AI year
Ask a local contractor about a comparable paid field opening
Cancel the children's paid summer holiday camp
Ask her sister for two childcare afternoons if affordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that full thinking AI in 2028 may run the office, but robots that can repair lines arrive around 2031. I would want an experienced lineworker beside every machine on its first wet-weather jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the office change and 48 when robots arrive. There are few line employers nearby, and a mortgage with almost no savings means a lost wage would hurt my family quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep every paid line shift I can and ask the depot what field jobs it expects to keep. In the first year after 2028 I would continue repairs, cancel the children's paid holiday camp for that summer and ask a local contractor about any opening with comparable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel afraid of the robot date, but I still expect to be working between 2028 and 2031. My partner and I would talk about the mortgage at the kitchen table after the children go to bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the children go instead of camp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could have them two afternoons a week if I cover the food and pick them up on time. I would ask her first, because I do not want to treat family help as free labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a contractor rather than a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contractor might have paid field work I can do now. I would consider paid apprenticeship-style training for a real opening, but I cannot leave wages for an uncertain certificate.

say: I would ask for **field robot demonstrations** before accepting staffing claims.
I would note **2031 AI** comes three years before hands-on robots.
think: At **51**, I may still have family bills and cannot assume retirement.
I would take **practical inspection training** only with paid time and real work.
do: Keep the present **paid rota** and request trial dates now.
In **2031**, watch a paid trial and apply for a comparable contractor opening if available.
feel: I feel **less cornered** with time and skeptical of untested devices.
S3.quote: A stack of online lessons at home would not make me safe.
fieldNote: Priya wants **live equipment** and a real instructor, showing resistance to screen-only learning even with more time.
Her **signed-contract condition** protects the mortgage and avoids treating a contractor inquiry as guaranteed employment.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2031 AI year
Apply for a comparable contractor field post if one is advertised
Take company-paid practical inspection training if it leads to a real post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that five years is enough to demand a proper demonstration before anybody calls a robot reliable. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the hands-on machines come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the office changes and 51 when robots reach our work. Our older child might be leaving school, but a family does not stop having bills at that age and I cannot assume I can retire at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for dates of field robot trials and keep working my present rota. In 2031 I would watch a trial on paid time, ask a local contractor about field vacancies and take a company-paid practical course only if it leads to one of those posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than with the two-year warning, but I do not like gambling on a new device. Show me a repair in freezing rain and I can decide what skill is still worth selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would need to teach how to inspect a robot-made joint at the pole, with a real instructor and live equipment. A stack of online lessons at home would not make me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the electricity company before the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave only for a signed contract with comparable wages. My mortgage cannot be paid with the hope that a contractor will find work later.

say: I would ask for **storm-tested machines** before changing crew staffing.
I would distinguish **2036 thinking AI** from line robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still owe on the family home and need paid work.
I would look for a **contractor post** if field hours actually decline.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** and make modest mortgage overpayments from standby.
In **2036**, review field hours and apply for posted contractor work if shifts fall.
feel: I feel **settled now** and cautiously watchful about 2039.
S4.quote: I would tell a new apprentice to learn the line craft and keep proof of every safety ticket.
fieldNote: Priya expects a long stretch of **paid physical work** and uses standby income for measured mortgage reduction.
She conditions a **contractor application** on observed lost shifts, and still values apprenticeship skills without promising permanent crew work.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Pay forty extra mortgage principal in months with two standby shifts
Apply for a posted contractor field role if crew shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a decade gives us time to see which machines work in storms, not just on a training pad. Full thinking AI arrives in 2036 and line-capable robots nearer 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the first date and 56 at the robot date. The children may have their own homes, but we could still owe on ours, and I have no reason to assume early retirement is funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep repairing lines and pay a little extra off the mortgage when standby shifts come. In 2036 I would look at the field-hours record, keep paid repairs while available and apply for a posted contractor role if our crew hours had started to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the next few years because I can still do honest field work. The later robot date worries me less than 2031 because there is time to pay the loan down and check actual job openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra could you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a month with two standby shifts I could put forty toward the principal without squeezing groceries. In a month without standby, I would pay the ordinary amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice to learn the line craft and keep proof of every safety ticket. I would not promise a lifetime on the same crew, because the machines may change that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot date around 2031 comes soon for a family with a mortgage and almost no savings. Paid practical training tied to a real field vacancy, honest trials in bad weather and steady wages until then would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the training happens during paid hours. A certificate is no use to my family if we miss a mortgage payment while I earn it.

headlineQuote: A certificate is no use to my family if we miss a mortgage payment while I earn it.
portrait: Priya is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and trusts printed permits, live tests and practical instruction.
Her **thin savings** make school costs and a missed standby payment immediately difficult.
Across the scenarios she protects **paid field work** and considers contractor jobs or training only with real wages.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves her family only about three years before robots may reach line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **practical training**, a real field vacancy and honest wet-weather trials would help her preserve mortgage payments.
